strengths: Clear and well-motivated pipeline: decomposing voxel captioning into (i) optimal image identification via encoding models, (ii) MLLM captioning, and (iii) LLM-based keyword extraction and sentence composition is a sensible modular design that can incorporate future vision/LLM advances without retraining.

Thorough quantitative evaluation: sentence-level and image-level prediction accuracy on 4 NSD subjects, shuffled-caption controls that validate the evaluation metric, comparisons against BrainSCUBA (with a careful, fair in-house reimplementation given unavailable code), and a hyperparameter ablation study (number of optimal images, number of keywords, extractor model).

The accuracy-vs-caption-length analysis (Figure 2 / A6) directly addresses the interpretability-accuracy trade-off, showing LaVCa reaches Concat-level accuracy with far fewer words; this is a convincing argument over naive concatenation.

Additional intra-voxel and inter-voxel diversity metrics and ROI-level shuffle analyses (e.g., OFA 3.3-fold accuracy drop under shuffling) support the claim that captions capture voxel-specific, not generic, selectivity, and yield interesting neuroscience observations about functional differentiation within ROIs.
Adequate statistical rigor: FDR correction for cortical maps, paired tests vs. BrainSCUBA, error bars, and per-subject results in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core ingredients (CLIP-based encoding weights, dot-product image search, captioning the optimal images, LLM summarization) closely follow BrainSCUBA and existing LLM-based neuron/feature description methods (SASC, MILAN, Dunlap et al.); the contribution is primarily an architectural recombination and better LLM utilization rather than a new idea.

Caption quality is questionable: many LaVCa captions in Figures 5, A7, A8-A11 are ungrammatical or incoherent (e.g., 'Car boot handbag baked in good polka dot patterned bicycle dessert', 'The person holding an animal mouth is a person wearing glasses'), a known failure mode of the MeaCap Sentence Composer; this undercuts the central 'interpretability' claim, and no human evaluation of caption fluency/faithfulness is provided.

The evaluation metric may be biased: Spearman correlation via Sentence-BERT similarity to COCO-style captions could favor captions that mimic COCO phrasing, and the fact that simple Concat achieves higher accuracy suggests the metric partly rewards verbosity; LaVCa's advantage over Concat is argued mainly through interpretability, which is assessed only qualitatively.

Hallucination risk is unquantified: LLM keyword extraction and the Sentence Composer can inject concepts not present in the optimal images (several examples show captions inconsistent with the top-49 image sets); there is no fidelity check between generated captions and the underlying optimal image sets, so claims about voxels encoding 'multiple distinct concepts' may partly reflect LLM confabulation.

Diversity metrics partially conflate diversity with caption length: LaVCa's intra-voxel lexical metrics (vocab size, length) being higher is expected for longer captions; the semantic variance differences are small (0.0199 vs 0.0160).

ROI-level quantitative analysis has a discrepancy (OFA accuracy of 0.0945 in text vs Table 2's 0.095±0.009 appears fine, but the PPA '1.4-fold' framing and mixed absolute accuracy levels across ROIs suggest the shuffle test mostly reflects signal strength rather than within-ROI heterogeneity per se).

Dependence on proprietary gpt-4o for the main results raises reproducibility concerns, and the improvement over the open Llama3.1-70B alternative, while real, is modest; no code release is stated in the main text.

strengths: The paper is well organized and clearly written, with a transparent four-step pipeline (encoding model → optimal image search → MLLM captioning → LLM keyword extraction and sentence composition) that is easy to follow and reproduce in principle.

Evaluation goes beyond qualitative examples: the authors use both sentence-level and image-level brain activity prediction with a shuffled-caption control, and report results across four NSD subjects and multiple voxel-selection thresholds (Tables 1, A2, A3).
An ablation study (Table A1) examines the number of optimal images, number of keywords, and choice of keyword extractor, giving some insight into design choices.

The ROI-level diversity analysis (Table 2, Figure 5) is a potentially interesting neuroscientific finding, suggesting fine-grained functional differentiation within classically defined ROIs such as OFA and PPA.
The comparison with BrainSCUBA is reasonably careful, including an in-house reimplementation with hyperparameter sweeps (Figure A1) when the original code was unavailable.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially an assembly of existing components (CLIP-based encoding, top-N image retrieval, an MLLM captioner, LLM keyword extraction following Dunlap et al. (2024), and MeaCap's Sentence Composer). The core contribution is a pipeline composition rather than a new technique or insight, and the delta over BrainSCUBA is largely 'replace the captioning model with a modern LLM stack.'

Circularity in the evaluation: CLIP representations are used for encoding, for optimal image selection, for keyword filtering, and again for sentence-level evaluation (via CLIP-text-derived sentence similarity), while image-level evaluation uses CLIP-Vision embeddings of images generated from the captions. Captions are thus implicitly optimized toward the very representational space used to score them, which inflates the apparent advantage over BrainSCUBA and makes the headline accuracy gains hard to interpret as evidence of true voxel selectivity.

The evaluation target is weak ground truth: voxel captions are validated by correlation against MS COCO captions of the stimuli, not against any independent characterization of voxel selectivity (e.g., human judgments, functional localizer checks, or held-out prediction of neural data). A caption that happens to match COCO caption style/distribution may score well without describing the voxel correctly.

Serious caption quality issues undermine the central 'interpretability' claim: many shown LaVCa captions are incoherent or ungrammatical (e.g., 'Car boot handbag baked in good polka dot patterned bicycle dessert', 'The person holding an animal mouth is a person wearing glasses', 'A keyboard made of sink covers from a laptop', 'Woodnut coloured blue eyes and a funny face painted by one person...'), and in several appendix examples (e.g., Figures A9, A11) LaVCa underperforms BrainSCUBA in accuracy. The paper does not confront or quantify these failure modes.

Diversity metrics are confounded by caption length and LLM style: LaVCa's higher vocabulary size, sentence length, and embedding variance largely follow from longer, LLM-generated captions rather than demonstrably richer characterization of neural tuning; longer captions trivially increase lexical/semantic spread.
Dependence on closed, proprietary components (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) for a core step weakens reproducibility and scientific control, and the ablation shows results are sensitive to the LLM used.

Statistical reporting is thin in places: significance is claimed via paired t-tests over voxels, which are highly non-independent (spatially autocorrelated), and the practical magnitude of improvement (~0.04 in rho) is modest relative to the added pipeline complexity and cost.

Some findings (e.g., that face ROIs show lower accuracy) are acknowledged but left speculative, and the paper does not establish that 'voxels representing multiple distinct concepts' reflects genuine neural encoding rather than artifacts of the keyword extraction and summarization procedure.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: voxel-level interpretation of DNN-based encoding models is an important, underexplored challenge, and the proposed pipeline (optimal image set discovery → MLLM captioning → LLM keyword extraction/filtering → sentence composition) is a sensible decomposition that removes the constraint of end-to-end captioning models used in BrainSCUBA.

Comprehensive quantitative evaluation: the paper evaluates at both sentence and image levels, across four NSD subjects, at multiple voxel-set sizes (Top-1000 to Top-10000), with appropriate controls (shuffled captions across voxels, shuffled captions within ROIs) and statistical testing (FDR correction, paired t-tests).

Convincing primary result: LaVCa consistently outperforms the reimplemented BrainSCUBA baseline (e.g., 0.246–0.306 vs. 0.207–0.264 sentence-level accuracy), and the shuffled control shows a large drop, supporting the validity of the evaluation metric.

Good interpretability-accuracy trade-off analysis (Figure 2 / Figure A6): the comparison with Concat-N baselines demonstrates that summarization retains accuracy while drastically reducing caption length (e.g., 11 vs. 680 words), addressing a key concern about verbose LLM outputs.

Thorough ablation study (Table A1) covering number of optimal images, number of keywords, and choice of keyword extractor (gpt-4o vs. Llama3.1-70B vs. TextGraphParser), with reasonable analysis of trends.

Neuroscientifically meaningful analysis: ROI-level within-region diversity analysis (Table 2, UMAP visualizations in OFA/PPA) goes beyond aggregate metrics and yields interpretable findings about fine-grained functional differentiation within classically defined ROIs.
Transparency about the in-house BrainSCUBA reimplementation, including temperature hyperparameter sweeps (Figure A1) and matched external image datasets to ensure a fair comparison.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the contribution is primarily a pipeline combination of existing components (CLIP-Vision encoding, MiniCPM-V, gpt-4o in-context keyword extraction from Dunlap et al., MeaCap's Sentence Composer, CLIP-based filtering). The individual techniques are not new; the paper is more of a careful systems/engineering contribution than an algorithmic advance.

Potential circularity in evaluation: both the encoding models and the sentence/image-level evaluation metrics are built on CLIP representations (CLIP-Vision for encoding and optimal image selection; CLIP-Text/Sentence-BERT similarity for scoring). Captions that align well with the CLIP embedding space may be systematically favored, which could inflate the advantage over BrainSCUBA, whose captioner is not CLIP-aligned. The paper does not adequately discuss or control for this.

Qualitative caption quality is inconsistent: several LaVCa captions shown in Figures 5, A8–A11 are grammatically broken or semantically dubious (e.g., 'Car boot handbag baked in good polka dot patterned bicycle dessert', 'The person holding an animal mouth is a person wearing glasses'). This raises concerns about whether the composed sentences faithfully reflect voxel selectivity or merely score well under the embedding-based metric, and no human evaluation is provided.

Fairness of the comparison: BrainSCUBA was reimplemented in-house with modified encoding weights (ridge regression instead of gradient descent) and a reduced image set (OpenImages only vs. OpenImages+LAION), and its code is unavailable; the reported gap may partly reflect implementation differences rather than fundamental method superiority. Comparison with SASC is only qualitative.

Diversity metrics may be confounded by caption length: LaVCa's intra-voxel lexical metrics (vocabulary size 11.4 vs. 6.09; length 11.9 vs. 6.19) partly reflect longer captions, so the claimed diversity gains are not fully disentangled from verbosity.

The central scientific claim that individual voxels 'simultaneously represent multiple distinct concepts' rests on caption content, which can be noisy LLM hallucination; independent validation (e.g., targeted stimulus experiments or held-out activation-based verification of individual concepts within a caption) is not provided.

Scale of brain-data analysis is modest (4 subjects, visual cortex only); generalization to other datasets/modalities (e.g., the fMRI speech dataset used by SASC) is not demonstrated despite being claimed as a strength of the framework.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem (interpreting single-voxel selectivity in the visual cortex) and clearly positions itself against prior work (BrainSCUBA, SASC, population-level semantic axes).

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this line of work: sentence-level and image-level prediction accuracy with permutation tests and FDR correction, cortical flatmap visualizations, diversity metrics (inter- and intra-voxel), ROI-level shuffled-caption controls, and cross-dataset generalization to BOLD5000.

The ablation studies are extensive and genuinely informative (encoding model variants, number of optimal images, number of keywords, MLLM/LLM choices, prompting strategies, sentence similarity model, sample-size and category-size sensitivity), supporting the design choices rather than just the final method.
The comparison against a simple concatenation baseline (Concat-N) makes the interpretability-accuracy trade-off explicit and quantifies that LaVCa retains accuracy while producing concise captions.
Reproducibility appears strong: checkpoints, prompts, hyperparameters, compute costs, and re-implementation details of the baseline are documented, and code is stated to be released.

The finding that category-selective ROIs (OFA, PPA) contain fine-grained, reproducible sub-selectivity across subjects is a scientifically interesting contribution beyond the engineering of the method.
weaknesses: The method is largely a pipeline assembly of existing components (CLIP embeddings + ridge regression, MLLM captioning, GPT-4o keyword extraction, MeaCap Sentence Composer, FLUX image generation); the conceptual novelty relative to BrainSCUBA/SASC is incremental.

The main quantitative comparison is only against BrainSCUBA (re-implemented in-house with modifications); SASC and other interpretable-encoding baselines are discussed but not empirically compared, weakening claims of superiority over prior approaches.

Several example captions (e.g., in Figure 5 and Appendix figures) are ungrammatical or semantically incoherent ('Woodnut coloured blue eyes and a funny face painted by one person showing a pig sticking out his tongue', 'A vintage car with sex clock stickers'), which undercuts the core claim of producing interpretable, human-readable voxel descriptions; no human evaluation of caption quality is provided.

The evaluation metric (Sentence-BERT similarity between voxel captions and COCO captions) may implicitly favor captions whose style/distribution resembles COCO captions; the circularity risk between caption generation and caption-based evaluation is only partially mitigated by the image-level metric.

The dependence on proprietary GPT-4o for keyword extraction and the 83-hour per-subject pipeline raise reproducibility and scalability concerns, and ablations show results are somewhat sensitive to LLM choice.

The central neuroscience claim of 'richer representational content' in ROIs relies heavily on qualitative UMAP/word-cloud analyses; the quantitative shuffled-within-ROI control shows distinctivity but not validity of the fine-grained interpretations.

Polish issues remain: typos ('LIMITAION'), a figure caption referring to UMAP2 for both axes (Figures A20-A23), inconsistent quotation marks in the text, and a blank reference URL in the reproducibility statement.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the method is described in enough detail (including prompts, checkpoints, hyperparameters, and compute costs in the appendix) to be largely reproducible.

The evaluation is more thorough than is typical for this line of work: predictions are assessed at both sentence and image levels, with shuffled-caption controls, permutation testing with FDR correction, extensive ablations over every pipeline component, sensitivity analyses over data size and category granularity, and a second dataset (BOLD5000) for cross-dataset generalization.
The re-implementation of BrainSCUBA with matched image datasets and hyperparameter sweeps (Figure A1) shows effort to make the comparison fair.

The framing distinguishing encoding-side interpretation from brain-to-text decoding is appropriate, and the ROI-level analysis (Table 2, cross-subject similarity) is a reasonable attempt at a quantitative claim about intra-ROI diversity.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior work. The core pipeline assembles existing components (CLIP encoding weights from BrainSCUBA, top-N optimal image retrieval, in-context keyword extraction from Dunlap et al. 2024, and the MeaCap sentence composer, mostly unchanged). SASC (Singh et al., 2023) already combines high-activation phrases with LLM summarization; LaVCa's contribution is essentially swapping in a stronger MLLM and GPT-4o and adding a fixed sentence composer. This is an incremental system-level refinement rather than a new methodological insight.

The evaluation metric has a potential circularity/bias problem. Voxel captions are generated from optimal images selected via the CLIP-Vision encoding weight, then scored by Sentence-BERT similarity to COCO captions. The pipeline is thus optimized end-to-end toward the very similarity measure used as 'accuracy,' and the reported gains over BrainSCUBA may partly reflect caption length, vocabulary diversity, and stylistic match to COCO captions rather than genuinely better capture of voxel selectivity. The Concat-N baseline (Figure 2) shows longer captions score higher, and the image-level metric still relies on the same CLIP feature space used for optimization.

Caption quality is questionable in the paper's own figures. Several showcased captions (e.g., 'The animal photos show how cute it is to comfort a red cardinal by touching zoo noses with bread', 'This is a fruit cake with banana icing and a decorative design' for a banana voxel, 'The digitally decorated room is a sign of the modern atmosphere') are ungrammatical or semantically incoherent, undermining the central claim of 'interpretable,' 'concise,' and 'accurate' captions. No human evaluation of caption plausibility or faithfulness to the optimal image sets is reported.

Dependence on a proprietary closed-source model (gpt-4o) for a core pipeline step weakens reproducibility and means results cannot be exactly reproduced even with the released code; the ablation with open LLMs shows a notable accuracy drop.

Scientific significance is overclaimed. The claim that LaVCa 'challenges long-standing assumptions about functional specialization' (e.g., OFA/PPA encode more than faces/places) is not new—distributed and mixed selectivity within these ROIs is well documented—and the supporting evidence (UMAP color diversity, noun-cluster counts) is largely qualitative and does not establish that the finer-grained selectivities are real rather than artifacts of the captioning pipeline.

The user-facing metric accuracy is low in absolute terms (e.g., ~0.21–0.31 at sentence level on top-5000 voxels, dropping to ~0.13–0.16 on top-10000), and the shuffle baseline indicates much of the predicted variance is modest; the practical interpretive value of a ρ ≈ 0.2 caption-level prediction is not established.

The manuscript has notable polish issues: several figure captions/text are garbled (missing closing quotes, 'LIMITAION', incomplete reproducibility URL, axis labels saying 'horizontal axis represents UMAP2, and the vertical axis represents UMAP2'), which suggests insufficient care and slightly reduces trust in the presentation.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated method: LaVCa decomposes voxel captioning into interpretable stages (encoding-model-based optimal image search, MLLM captioning, LLM keyword extraction, Sentence Composer), decoupling image selection from caption generation and enabling modularity across backbones.

Evaluation is more rigorous than typical for this line of work: caption accuracy is assessed at both sentence and image levels (the latter controlling for non-visual linguistic confounds), with permutation tests and FDR correction, shuffled-caption controls, and results reported consistently across four NSD subjects and multiple top-N voxel selections.

Extensive ablations (encoding model variants, contrastive VLMs, number of optimal images/keywords, MLLM choice, extraction model, prompting strategy, sentence similarity model) plus data-size sensitivity analyses and an independent cross-dataset validation on BOLD5000 with cross-dataset reproducibility of ROI-level semantic patterns.

Scientifically interesting finding: revealing richer, heterogeneous representational content within category-selective ROIs (OFA, PPA) that prior literature characterized as selectively tuned to single categories, supported by both qualitative (UMAP/word clouds) and quantitative (ROI-shuffle, multi-cluster) analyses.
Strong reproducibility: complete model/checkpoint lists, prompts, hyperparameters, compute details, and a public code release statement.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the pipeline is primarily a careful assembly of existing components (CLIP encoding, MiniCPM-V captioning, GPT-4o keyword extraction from Dunlap et al., MeaCap sentence composition); the conceptual contribution over BrainSCUBA/SASC is real but modest.

The only substantive baseline is BrainSCUBA (re-implemented in-house with differences in regression method and projection dataset, acknowledged by the authors); no comparison against SASC or other neuron-labeling methods on the same task weakens the claim of superiority over 'previous approaches'.
GPT-4o (closed-source, API-only) is a core component, limiting reproducibility over time and raising questions about whether gains stem from LLM capability rather than the proposed pipeline design.

The headline quantitative gains are modest in absolute terms (e.g., 0.246 vs 0.207 sentence-level at top-5000) and the image-level evaluation depends on FLUX-generated voxel images, which introduces an additional generative model's biases into the metric; circularity risk from CLIP-based filtering/selection and CLIP-based image evaluation is not fully analyzed.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'challenging long-standing assumptions about functional specialization' is largely supported by qualitative UMAP/word-cloud observations and moderate accuracy drops under ROI shuffling; the k-means (k=6) noun clustering analysis is somewhat ad hoc.

Writing and polish issues remain: typos ('LIMITAION'), recurring grammatical slips ('functional specialization across inter-voxel', inconsistent singular/plural use), and missing URL in the reproducibility statement.
Computational cost is high (~83 h for 20,000 voxels per subject on 8 A100s), which limits practical scalability, though it is at least documented.
